this game is incredibly close to not being absolutely atrocious to play its upsetting, the dodge timings seem specifically designed to slam your head in to enemies or attacks. money is so scarce that without either a optimal room layout or one of the rare rooms that gives you excess money, or one of the incredibly rare mobs that drop about 5 floors worth of gold, you can't afford the basic damage upgrade per floor, let alone anything else, including the extra shop per floor that usually spawns. enemy / yourself hitboxes are absolutely whack as well (baseball bat swing is about 1.5x the length of the actual animation). and hot damn the tank boss, I've beaten it a few times, but a lot of potential positions result in a 100% chance of taking damage, which you can deal with sure, but just like invisible whack a mole, its not an enjoyable experience trying to work out what exact timings you need to slip through the millisecond long gap. you can apparently melee the normal twin to avoid the slide going off, but across the multiple attempts I've tried this, It never worked. Not saying the game doesn't have good points, art style is great, the many comedy weapons are funny (albeit most of them are useless, which sucks because most ranged weapons aren't good as is.) and the actual format of the bosses is great, I've beaten magnolia hit-less a good few times, which rewards you with extra max health, which is great. the multiple shops that spawn and optional bonuses such as the deal demon (who, outside of the invisible enemies deal has good negative / bonus deals) are nice, albeit due to economy being a mess you usually can't use them. I'll keep it installed and pay attention to updates, but unless the tank boss and either item prices or enemy gold drop rates change, I doubt i'll try this again.

As much as i'd love to give the game a good rating i simply can't, there are way too many issues both in the game balance and the game fun aspect Consider my opinion is after finishing the game once, but sadly not more than that as it is no longer a fun experience for me The pro's: It's a free game, there are no expectations to be had here, we did not pay for it, the devs went above and beyond with the art style Lots of guns to choose from, and a lot of them have very unique and fun ways to shoot The Normal enemies are easy to handle 1v1 with some exceptions The interactions have lots of personality in them which is very rare in the games we have today There are lots of characters to choose from, and 2 of them don't require you to beat the game(shed is very easy to get) The music is absolutely perfect, especially for the last stage bosses However...now the cons, and the main reasons why i would not recommend the game to a normal person that has the goal of finishing the game The guns are completely unbalanced, lots of them being unusable for the last boss fight, with only a very select few that can even deal with the last boss in a acceptable amount of time(rpg,sniper,golden revolver,the last aid, big dawg), i would love to see the devs balance them out against the bosses, i feel like a lot of the guns are fun against normal enemies, but right now the main issue is the fact there's very little weapons that can be fun against bosses, considering it's rng when it comes to what weapon you get, i found myself restarting runs tens of times just because i didn't get a good enough weapon, which ruined the fun i had from the game The hp system is way too punishing in multiple ways, depending on the run and your luck taking 1 single hit can be permanent for the entire run unless you buy healing, this makes small mistakes impossible to fix sometimes, health drops from enemies are not something you can count on, and there are 2 special shops that are hp based, however because of how punishing the hp system is, these shops are practically not an option, especially the gambling machine I would love it if the devs gave us more health, or allowed us to turn on game modifiers so we can choose our own difficulty after finishing the game once, even fully healing the player on each floor would be a choice, but the game balance would be difficult with it, either way making hp easier to get would improve the game a lot, it's fine for the game to be hard as long as it's FUN, min-maxing hp for the entire run, even if it's on average 10-15m is not fun The non boss enemies are fun to fight, but there's an issue with some specific combination of them where you either kill them fast enough(here we get back into the gun rng) or you have to take some damage(and here we get back into the hp system), it's not an issue that happens a lot, but it happens enough for it to become unfun and annoying at best, especially because there's not enough room to move and dodge, which is the next point i am going to make There's no way to place it, you will always feel like there's not enough room, especially during boss fights A perfect example of what i consider are the best boss fights are(warning slight spoiler ahead) The first, third and the first stage of the 4th boss The first boss has a very nice movement pattern, there's enough room to dodge and to learn it, we're not overstimulated by all the atacks and projectiles so we can focus on shooting and dodging The second boss is terrible, even after learning it's patterns and no hitting it i still am not having fun when fighting it, it simply takes too much space and leaves us with barely any spot to fight, my usual strategy is just to melee the first one quickly while shooting so i can then enjoy the tank fight, either making the first one slide way less or making the tank appear as a second stage could be options to balance it out The third boss is what i would consider the most fun one in the game, it has a very good and readable pattern, the atacks while at first are very hard, once you learn them they are satisfying to dodge, it's hard enough so that you have to stay engaged in the fight and not autopilot, and the boss gives you plenty of room to move because it stays high in the air, if there's one boss that should be an example for all the others, this one should be it The 4th boss is one that i love and hate, i love their first stage, even if there's no guidance on how to avoid some atacks(seriously how do you guys communicate to the player that they must crouch to dodge the spear...have i missed something...?) they are manageable, they are at the limit of what i would consider balanced hard but fun, and beating them is FUN...but then we get into the second stage... which has multiple issues, it goes beyond the limit of hard but fun, there's too many projectiles and atacks, too many things happening, the player is already overstimulated by the atacks alone, we get back into the issue of not enough space but it's not as bad as the second boss, i love the slown down atacks but there's way too much happening, i consider it's even harder than the last stage The last stage is more fun than the second, but there's one issue with it...the player doesn't know how big their hit box is, it makes the fight feel unfair when you do it the first time, we're bringing something new and changing something very important(how the model looks) at a very late stage of the game, however this is important to know if the devs are reading this, it IS a very good final stage, and i beg of you to not see it as something that shouldn't be done again because it gave the boss fight SO much personality, i absolutely loved it the first time i got to it, instead see it as something that requires a bit of mental prep time for the player, one way to do this is to have the player do a bit of dodging before the boss battle, maybe have them dodge the rays for a bit before the boss appears? Now onto something else, the gold...honestly i'm mixed up here, sometimes it's way too much, other times it's way too little...i'd like it if it was more consistent with how much we get, there's some runs where i couldn't buy the dmg upgrade on the first floor even after doing it perfectly and others where i had enough gold to buy everything The biggest issue i have on my side is the fact there's no boss trial mode or one way to get to the final boss quicker, even if it means i have less items or that i do practically no dmg, learning the boss patterns is very important, but it's so not fun when each try means spending 15 minutes to get there...IF you get the good rng weapons to even get there I won't dive into the melee and dodge mechanics as other people already talked about it enough The game has some big issues with balancing and rng, i think it can be fixed but i don't expect it will be fixed Should you try the game? 100% Should you try to finish the entire game? no Is it fun? yes for the first hours, no if you actually get into the game Consider that my opinion is based on what i like about games, and what i find fun, thank you for reading and have a good day!

My opinion's really mixed. The gameplay is fun, but I have a few big complaints to list; - The rooms are small and uncomfortable with how far you dodge roll and how large your hitbox is. - There's not enough money, the best thing you can possibly buy on any floor is a damage upgrade (which each floor has exactly one of, and there's 4 floors, so each one COUNTS) because everything else you can buy kinda gets handed to you naturally. Half the time you can't even afford that damage upgrade because there's not enough enemies. - The bosses are hell. I think they break the pace in a way. You have to play very precisely to win boss fights, and if you don't you either die very quickly or you're crippled for the next layer of the game that features new and unfamiliar enemies. Tank twins are the worst about this because their attacks just aren't fair-- 1/3 of the already TINY arena's taken up by the Tank That Kills You With Contact Damage For Daring To Dodge Roll and the other 2/3 is where the other person is spamming melee attacks and slow projectiles. And then the person on the tank pulls out a sniper rifle to force your attention off of the other one. This is the second boss in the game. I like the game's sense of humor, I love the game's music and visuals, I like the gameplay, but the game's bosses feel unfair and what you get between them is a bit too RNG-dependent even for a roguelike

10/10，五分给百合，五分给美术，零分给操作。 优点很明显，但同时缺点更明显 首先游戏的画面确实不错，作为一款免费的像素风游戏有这样看着很舒服的画面属实很不错，里面的妹子们都很可爱，尤其是靶场的小姐姐（doge）其次，枪械倒是有不少搞怪有趣的，比如发射骨头或者鱼，又或者是电视机蹦出来小人，看的出来时有设计的。 但是更大的还是缺点部分。第一点，角色的性能很低，虽说可以跳可以翻滚，但是真正在战斗中你不会经常使用跳跃去应对敌人，因为空间很小，跳跃意味着将自己受击面积扩大，负面收益高于正面收益。第二点，翻滚的无敌帧很短，这点在第一个BOSS那里体现的很清楚，第一个BOSS抬手很快，如果你在躲闪攻击的时候慢了一点点，就会在翻滚一小段的时候被打到，翻滚结束的时候也同理，很容易就会翻滚到敌人的子弹上面，这就让人玩的时候很郁闷，本来应该能躲掉的攻击却因为翻滚无敌帧太短而躲不掉，而躲不掉的代价就是扣血，这就引入了第三点，血量的补给太少。基本上只有两个商店能购买补血的道具，但是钱币也是很珍贵的资源，假如购买补血道具基本上就没钱买加攻击的道具了，血量在道中掉率又十分感人，这就陷入了一个矛盾：我要是买补血道具，攻击太低就会更容易受伤，但是不补血也容易暴毙，所以然人很纠结。第四点，BOSS的设计上，美术效果肯定是很顶的，但是作为第一个BOSS，拿剑的小姐姐属实有点难了，抬手很短就使得第一次打大概率打不过，基本上不交几次学费是打不过的，这我忍了，但是你第二关的BOSS是什么鬼，BOSS有两个，本来空间就不大，两个BOSS一下子占据了近一般的屏幕，一个是炮台又能追踪，一个机动能力强活动范围又大，在加上角色的性能，导致在打这俩BOSS的时候所做的任何一个跳跃任何一个翻滚风险都很高，当然能看出来BOSS攻击是有规律的，但是这学费属实有点离谱了，俩小时硬是没打过第二大关。 总的来说作为一款免费游戏确实也做到了他该做到的部分，但是还是有点不尽人意，作者也说了最后一次更新之后就不会更新了，所以想要调难度估计是没得搞了，只能菜就多练了（doge）

The game is really good. The NPC variety is fun and I love each one of them, there are many different guns that are each fun and exciting to use (love the Ultrakill references!!!) The art is great and doesn't suffer from inconsistent pixels, has interesting character and item designs, and different rooms that require you to gamble with your life. You will have fun playing this! The one major complaint I have is contact hitboxes. 90% of the damage I take from Magnolia is just from exiting a dash that barely passed her while she is standing completely still, walking into her after I'm cornered, etc. Games like Cave Story maintain their difficulty while making it feel fair by removing most boss's contact hitboxes and having their attacks do the damage instead. Certain enemies like the trash can in the second level are completely immobile but still have contact damage, despite throwing projectiles and summoning another enemy on death. I think this game would benefit from that changing. Enemies also weirdly clip to platforms above them sometimes, and can still damage you during dash recovery, which works against gameplay consistency. Otherwise, incredible game and I'm surprised it's completely free. It's the little things that hold it back and make it more of a hassle to play.

Steam is drowning in thousands of lazy, low-effort 2D platformers, and "Rabbit Hole" is yet another one. I'm not kidding, there's over 17,000 platformers on Steam, almost all of them are garbage, amateur kitbashes. This is not one of the good ones. This is a poorly made pixelcrap platformer shooter brawler where you control a girl called "Disc", get transported somewhere called the "Rabbit Hole" so I guess that's like an Alice thing or something. You do a lot of shooting, unlock some characters and weapons, but really the presentation here is woefully bad. Balance isn't great either, fighting areas are tiny. Maybe a "ultra easy" story difficulty mode would have helped the game do a little better, but nothing can really save pixelcrap. Platforming is an old, mostly dead genre, and this lacklustre experience, while it doesn't have an upfront cost, isn't saving the genre... it's no surprise this failed to capture any attention from gamers in the era of immersive 3D gaming. This looks a lot like it was designed for consoles, but released on Steam instead by mistake. While this is on PC, it has all the hallmarks and deficiencies of a console game, from the clunkier than needed control scheme to the less than cutting edge graphics. There's 10's of thousands of PC games on Steam, and PC gamers deserve only the best. This might not appeal to many gamers due to the lack of PC-centric design. It's unclear why this never made it to the video game console appliances it seems to have been designed for. On top of all that, the pixelcrap "art" here isn't even used consistently throughout the game. If you're going to commit to a terrible aesthetic, you at least have to be consistent about it. The one thing you could hope for when developers insult gamers with pixelcrap is authenticity, and they failed at that, too. This also means the developer knew they could have done better, but maybe they chose not to, on purpose... that's a massive disservice to gamers. The developer chose not to do the job of a real game developer and create meaningful bespoke levels, narrative based gameplay progression and so on. Instead, they decided that "Procgen IS content!" and lazily tried to use procgen algorithms to create infinite, samey, repetitive, soulless levels, because that's a lot less work. As a result of this poor decision, the game gets tired and repetitive almost immediately. Developers must learn that procgen is a terrible substitute for creating real content. It should not be used as "ez-mode" for content creation, as the developer tried to do here. Now onto pricing and value. They have their hand out for a $7 USD "donation" for this as you're expected to give them money from buying empty DLC from Steam... digital panhandling. Like the homeless guys who splash dirty water on your windscreen at the traffic lights. No thanks. Despite having no up-front cost, this failed to appeal to the 130 million+ gamers on Steam. SteamDB shows this peaked at less than 100 concurrent players... they couldn't even break three figures! Even though it's free, it's a dismal reception, but it's easy to see why gamers rejected it. Rabbit Hole is a psychological horror game that focuses less on direct terror and more on creating a constant feeling of unease and emotional instability. Rather than overwhelming players with nonstop jump scares or action-heavy encounters, the game slowly pulls them into a disturbing world where reality becomes increasingly unreliable. From the beginning, the atmosphere feels uncomfortable in a deliberate and carefully controlled way. Strange environments, unsettling imagery, and fragmented storytelling combine to create an experience that feels more like descending into a nightmare than simply surviving a horror scenario. The game succeeds because it understands that fear can be far more effective when it develops gradually through tension and uncertainty. One of the most impressive aspects of Rabbit Hole is its environmental atmosphere. Nearly every location carries a sense of isolation and hidden danger, even during moments where nothing actively threatening is happening. The game constantly creates the feeling that something is wrong beneath the surface. Dim lighting, distorted architecture, eerie silence, and subtle visual abnormalities make exploration feel tense at all times. Instead of relying on obvious horror clichés, the environments themselves become a source of psychological discomfort. Players often feel nervous simply walking through ordinary hallways or abandoned rooms because the game establishes such an oppressive mood. The narrative structure also contributes heavily to the experience. Rabbit Hole avoids straightforward storytelling and instead presents its plot through fragmented details, symbolic imagery, environmental clues, and unsettling encounters. This approach encourages players to piece together the story gradually while questioning whether the events unfolding around them are real or products of psychological collapse. The ambiguity works well because it keeps players engaged emotionally while maintaining a strong sense of mystery. The game rarely explains everything directly, which allows the unsettling atmosphere to linger even after major revelations occur. Visually, Rabbit Hole uses style and atmosphere more effectively than raw graphical power. The environments often feel surreal, as though familiar places have been twisted into disturbing dreamscapes. Lighting effects and visual distortions help reinforce the sense of mental instability that defines much of the game’s horror. Certain scenes become memorable not because of graphic violence or monster design, but because of how strange and psychologically uncomfortable they feel. The game frequently manipulates perception by subtly changing environments or introducing disturbing imagery in unexpected ways, making players constantly question their surroundings. Sound design is another major reason the horror works so effectively. The audio creates tension through unsettling ambient noises, distant echoes, distorted sounds, and moments of near silence that make players anticipate danger even when nothing appears on screen. The game understands how powerful subtle sound design can be in psychological horror. Small noises often feel more threatening than loud scares because they create uncertainty rather than immediate shock. Wearing headphones significantly improves the experience since the positional audio and environmental effects contribute heavily to immersion. The pacing is intentionally slow and methodical, which may not appeal to everyone but fits the overall tone extremely well. Rabbit Hole prioritizes atmosphere and psychological pressure over constant action. Exploration and observation are central parts of the experience, and the game often allows tension to build naturally before introducing major horror moments. This slower structure helps the unsettling atmosphere sink in more deeply because players spend long stretches immersed in uncomfortable environments without immediate relief. Fans of psychological horror will likely appreciate this approach far more than players looking for fast-paced survival gameplay. Puzzle elements are integrated throughout the experience and generally support the game’s themes rather than feeling disconnected from them. Many puzzles require careful observation of the environment and encourage players to pay close attention to details that may initially seem insignificant. Some challenges are satisfying to solve because they reinforce immersion and narrative progression, though a few sections may feel overly obscure depending on the player’s tolerance for abstract puzzle design. Fortunately, the puzzles rarely become frustrating enough to completely interrupt the atmosphere. One of the game’s most effective qualities is how it constantly plays with the player’s perception. Locations change unexpectedly, visual details shift subtly, and familiar spaces become distorted without warning. This instability creates psychological tension because players never fully trust what they are seeing. The horror feels more personal as a result, since the game suggests that the true danger may come from the protagonist’s deteriorating mental state rather than from any physical threat alone. This uncertainty becomes one of the strongest sources of fear throughout the experience. Despite its many strengths, Rabbit Hole does have flaws. The abstract storytelling can occasionally become too vague, making certain narrative moments feel confusing instead of intriguing. Players who prefer clearly explained plots may struggle with the intentionally fragmented presentation. Technical limitations also appear at times, including rough animations and occasional performance inconsistencies that reveal the game’s smaller production scale. While these issues rarely ruin the experience, they can momentarily weaken immersion during important scenes. The slower pacing may also divide audiences. Players expecting frequent enemy encounters or action-oriented horror sequences may find some sections uneventful. Rabbit Hole is much more interested in creating emotional discomfort and psychological tension than providing constant thrills. For some players this creates a far more memorable experience, while others may feel the game moves too cautiously. What ultimately makes Rabbit Hole stand out is its commitment to psychological horror built around atmosphere and emotional unease rather than spectacle. The game succeeds in creating a world that feels deeply unsettling without relying excessively on predictable scares. It captures the sensation of gradually losing trust in reality while forcing players to explore environments filled with tension and uncertainty. Even after finishing the game, many of its surreal images and oppressive moments remain memorable because of how effectively they disturb the player psychologically rather than simply startling them. Rabbit Hole may not redefine horror gaming, but it delivers a compelling and immersive descent into paranoia and instability that fans of slow-burning psychological horror will likely appreciate. Its atmosphere, sound design, and surreal storytelling combine to create an experience that feels haunting long after the credits roll. Rating: 8/10

firstly, it's a free game, which is a massive benefit. the sountrack is great, the variety of weapons is nice, the character designs are all appealing, the game's presentation is generally excellent. unfortunately, there's just a buttload of minor flaws that really stack up to make an often irritating experience. you're unable to pause while there are still enemies in the current room. huh?? the rooms are far too narrow to warrant having a set-distance dodge roll. it would feel much better to have even a slight amount of influence. also, the dodge roll really ought to have invulnerability on the first frame. this, combined with the player's hurt box being fatter than it probably should be, often results in taking damage that doesn't feel fair. you'll roll into a projectile that was lingering on the other side of the room, or you'll make contact with an enemy that probably shouldn't even be dealing contact damage. there's a lack of room variety. you will see consecutive identical rooms frequently. there's not much variation between runs at all. sometimes, i'm unable to see enemies or their projectiles past some of the more flashy effects that my guns produce. guns don't automatically reload when the magazine is empty. you have to click an additional time or press the reload key, for some reason. about the melee potentially being overpowered, i'm not sure i agree. it's true that it's far more effective during the early game than most guns, especially before any damage upgrades, but later on i think the balance smooths out. i see many claiming that the tank twins are overpowered, but that's really not the case. my first few times fighting them, i noticed the difficulty spike, but it's more than possible to get comfortable with their attack patterns. the real issue is just that the room becomes even more cramped with that tank in there.
